title: Kannappa's eye
hookLine: a hunter who worships Shiva all wrong, and all right
carry: shiva looks at the love, not the rules

cards: Every morning a priest climbs a hill to a small shrine of Shiva, and every morning he finds a mess. Bits of meat on the stone. Flowers that look like they've been in someone's hair.
Water spat everywhere. He cleans it, does the worship properly, and goes home upset. Someone is worshiping here, and doing it all wrong.

teach.b: Today the path crosses to the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva. Tradition counts sixty-three, and their lives are told in a long Tamil work, the Periya Puranam.

They're kings, housewives, a potter, a washerman, and today, a hunter, Tinnan. Tracking in the hills, he finds the shrine, and something in him breaks open. He knows no rules, so he worships the way a hunter loves.
He carries water in his mouth, because he has no pot. He brings flowers in his hair, because his hands hold his bow.

teach.h: WATER IN HIS MOUTH, MEAT TASTED FIRST.
teach.b: And he brings meat he has roasted and tasted first, so only the best goes to Shiva. That's the mess. In the story, Shiva tells the priest in a dream to hide and watch.
So the priest is hiding the day the image's eye starts to bleed. Tinnan's herbs don't help, so he takes an arrow, digs out his own eye, and presses it into place.

teach.h: HIS OWN EYE FOR THE BLEEDING ONE.
teach.b: The bleeding stops. Then the image's other eye starts to bleed. Tinnan sets his foot on the spot, to find it once he's blind, and lifts the arrow to his other eye.
And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and stops him. He's called Kannappa, a name tied to his eye.

It isn't a call to harm yourself; if you ever have thoughts like that, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Andal wore the garland first; now a hunter tastes the meat first.
In the Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it.
That's bhakti at its boldest: God looks at the love before the rules.
The story didn't change temple rules, but it tells every nervous beginner what matters most, and the priest who knows every rule is the one sent to watch.

how: Shaiva Hindus in Tamil Nadu honor the Nayanars in temples, often with images of them in a row, and Kannappa is especially remembered at the Shiva temple of Srikalahasti.

o: wandering monks who beg from town to town
the hunters who guard a hill shrine of Shiva
the Tamil saints of Shiva, sixty-three by tradition

games.q: the hunter's worship — tap the pairs.
p: told in a dream to hide and watch

s: the Nayanars were all priests and scholars
they included kings, housewives, a potter, a washerman and a hunter.
Kannappa gave his own eye when the image's eye bled
and he was ready to give the second before Shiva stopped him.
the priest chased the hunter away
in the story, Shiva tells the priest to hide and watch.

games.q: you're the hunter. you've given one eye, and now the image's other eye is bleeding. what do you do?
o: run for help from the priest.
set your foot on the spot and lift the arrow to your second eye.
games.why: he marks the spot with his foot so he can find it blind, and Shiva's hand stops him. the love was already enough.

practice: Hindus offer what they have: a flower, a leaf, a little water. Today, offer one small thing, even a glass of water, to Shiva, or to God by whatever name you use, the way Kannappa did: no rulebook, full heart.
If you don't pray, give one person something small today with your whole attention.

wordCard.voice: The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva, whose lives the Periya Puranam tells. Kannappa is the hunter who offered his own eye.

orig.note: Tamil: the name for the saints of Shiva in the Tamil tradition.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva looks at the love, not the rules. A hunter with no rulebook, remembered as a saint. Day nine hundred ten, done.
